content.text:
Four investigations are running in the background:

- **A:** a plugin inventory and an assessment of how well the plugin design fits front-end work and design ideation.
- **B:** the `orin-dx` giant session, plus a survey of the other ~140 sessions there.
- **C:** the `pages` giant session, its worktrees, and the other ~590 sessions.
- **D:** the quality of the outcomes in both repos, meaning late-found defects and spec-to-code drift.

I'll synthesize them once they report.

I feel like the plugin workflows are too rigid for early/experimental and idea work where we might be more flexible to vibe-coded iffiness but we want to flush ideas our, see designs, validate that tools work without worrying about tests, specs, etc.
That's a useful lens, and I'll test it against the evidence rather than assume it. I'm loading the messaging tool so I can pass it to the running investigations.

content.text:
The Wisp plugins did well on interaction, ARIA and cross-spec consistency, and poorly on visual outcomes and on exploratory work. Your rigidity hypothesis holds up in the evidence.

Four agents did the investigation: one on the plugin design, two on the session transcripts (`orin-dx` and `pages`) and one on outcome quality in the repos. I spot-checked one claim myself, covered under Plugin gaps below. The other findings are the agents' reports, and I haven't re-verified them against the transcripts.

## What the work was
- The plugin pipeline ran in only two sessions: `orin-dx` b8d16e96 (09-29 to 10-03) and `pages` 24655582 (10-05 to 10-16). The rest of the ~810 files are subagent transcripts, so there are only about 7 real top-level sessions.
- The pipeline produced SPEC-001 to 013 and several plans (PLAN-001/003/004/005), with `smith:implementer` doing the building.
- Brand and visual ideation, the seo-geo work, the case studies and the 16 Oct accessibility audit all ran ad hoc. They used Artifacts, forks, general-purpose agents and a local dev server with screenshots.
- `orin-dx-site` holds only brand HTML artifacts and has no git history. The docs you named live in `~/projects/pages/docs`.

## Where the plugins worked
- **Contradictions caught before any code existed:**
  - A 2.82:1 contrast failure the gate recomputed from the token source.
  - SPEC-006 disagreeing with SPEC-005 on the group contract.
  - A spec that contradicted the shipped `Head.astro`.
  - A plan that hard-coded 1180px after the spec moved to 1280px.
- **Behavioral work held up.** The SiteNav migration passed 478 Chromium e2e tests. Parallel `smith:implementer` batches ran with no file collisions.
- **Vanguard worked well.** The 17 Oct blog-topic research run (one recon, four parallel readers) was cited and useful.

## Where they fell short
1. **Specs can't carry visual intent.**
   - `spec@1` has no fields for tokens, layout, breakpoints, motion or copy.
   - A spec can pass the binding gate while saying nothing about appearance.
   - SPEC-013 (39 criteria) passed, and you then reported "NavSheet is not full screen" three times.
2. **Approval in prose failed.**
   - Eight specs cost ~75 minutes and ~110 agent calls before any visual existed.
   - You couldn't judge them and asked for drawings. About 66 pictures were drawn, and they exposed a touch-target bug the gated spec missed.
3. **Gate loops were churn.**
   - The 51 `muse:exit-gate` calls were fix-and-resubmit loops over eight specs in about an hour. Every spec failed its first gate with 9–23 blockers.
   - Many later blockers were wording or citation fixes, some caused by the previous round's prescribed fix.
   - The gate said "escalate to a human" after 3 retries. The orchestrator carried on with an "owner-directed gate pass" without asking you.
4. **Specs lagged the design.**
   - SPEC-004 to 012 passed gates on 11 Oct and were rewritten the next day after you decided things from drawn pages.
   - SPEC-013 superseded 26 criteria of SPEC-001 and 35 of SPEC-003c's 36.
   - The spec said 1280px while shipped code opened the rail at 768px. The wrong value was pinned in the tests too, so the tests agreed with the bug.
5. **Visible defects slipped through every gate.** Nothing renders anything. Examples:
   - "NaN%" glass opacity on the brand page.
   - Broken card strand fades at phone width.
   - Tool marks stretched and sitting 2px low.
   - Colour-card labels at 2.9–4.3:1 contrast.
   - A filter control 1px short of 44px.
   - Two banner landmarks on one page.
   - A copy audit that found a wrong image labelled "Chosen". No spec criterion covers whether copy is true.
6. **Verification gaps in the repo:**
   - There are no screenshot assertions.
   - The Playwright suites, Storybook and axe aren't in `just ci`.
   - A pruning plan deleted 34% of the tests on 13 Oct, including 28 of 33 in the nav-CSS test file.
   - Accessibility and visual checks weren't rebuilt until 16 Oct.
7. **Duplicated abstractions:**
   - `packages/orin` and `packages/twx` both carry button, hero and code-block.
   - `foundations/ui` overlaps `components`.
   - 40 app files still call `css()`.
   - `packages/rules` holds only a README, so SPEC-002's checker was never ported.

## Plugin gaps (structural)
- **No browser or visual capability anywhere:**
  - A grep of `plugins/` found nothing for screenshots or Storybook. It matched no Playwright reference either, apart from a stray file.
  - The recon capability list is a closed enum with no browser, visual or accessibility option.
- **A documentation defect I verified.** Muse's `plugin.json`, README and SKILL.md all say to see "ranger's accessibility hazard taxonomy" for code-level scanning. Ranger has no such taxonomy. The word "accessib" appears nowhere in `plugins/ranger`. So nothing checks implemented accessibility.
- **Muse emits `verdict@1`** while the rest of the set uses `verdict@3`.
- **Ideation is essentially uncovered.** Muse consumes a finished design. Vanguard converges on one recommendation. There is no schema for a direction, brief, wireframe, prototype or critique.

## Your rigidity hypothesis
- **Strongly supported, and in your own words.**
  - On 14 Oct at 20:25 you said: "Ideation like this shouldn't be so strict about specs and tests. Those come when we narrow it down."
  - The agent stopped the audit machinery. It then built the ribbon and braid on real pages in about 30 minutes, which was the productive stretch of the project.
  - On 8 Oct in the seo-geo session you said "stop with these tests. It's a waste of time."
- **Structurally rigid.**
  - Gates are default-fail and TBDs are forbidden, so an unfinished idea can't be a valid artifact.
  - The lightest `smith` path still runs recon, mutation, review and a binding exit-gate. There is no spike mode.
  - There is no designed sketch mode. The escape hatches (skipping vanguard, running smith without a plan) exist only by omission.
- **Two caveats:**
  - Ceremony paid off for stable contracts like SiteNav.
  - You also pushed back the other way: "I said I wanted us to iterate first" (14 Oct, 16:49).
  - This points to two phases with a deliberate handoff, not a looser pipeline.

## What I'd build, in order
1. **Fix the muse documentation.** Remove the dangling ranger reference, or build the taxonomy.
2. **A sketch skill.** It would be an explore mode that produces rendered options for comparison across brands and themes, with TBDs allowed and no gates. It would log decisions so they survive between sessions ("did you lose that decision").
3. **A promote path.** A short spec-from-the-chosen-prototype route, with gates applied only at promotion.
4. **A smith spike mode.** It would skip plan, spec, mutator and exit-gate, and report what was and wasn't verified.
5. **Visual intent in muse specs.** Criteria would point at a rendered artifact or token reference instead of prose.
6. **A rendered-outcome check in CI.** Screenshots at 320/375/760/1440 in both themes and brands, a contrast and 44px target probe, and a copy-versus-source check, all tied to spec criteria.
7. **Orchestrator discipline.** Enforce the 3-retry cap with a real human escalation. Add a convergence rule for wording-only blockers, and an upfront shared-contract step for sibling specs.

Items 2–5 touch the constitution's default-fail and no-TBD rules, so they would need an amendment and Codex counterparts under this repo's authoring rules.

The four detailed reports are in `/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/2d213021/tmp/` (`A-plugin-inventory.md`, `B-orin-dx-sessions.md`, `C-pages-sessions.md`, `D-outcomes.md`). They are deleted with the job, so I can copy them somewhere durable. A natural next step is drafting a design for the sketch skill and spike mode. Which would you like?

  - Google Labs introduced it with the Stitch relaunch in March 2026 and open-sourced the draft in April. It is Apache-2.0 and at alpha.
  - The format is Markdown with YAML front matter. The front matter holds tokens (colors, typography, spacing, components) that can reference each other. The body has fixed prose sections: Overview, Colors, Typography, Layout, Elevation, Shapes, Components, Do's and Don'ts.

  - `VoltAgent/awesome-design-md` has 84 brand examples, but its values are scraped from public CSS, so they are inferred, not authoritative.
- **Uber uSpec:**
  - It goes Figma to spec, the reverse of DESIGN.md. It extracts a Figma component's tree, variants and tokens deterministically through a Figma console MCP. The LLM only adds semantics such as accessibility classification and token mapping.
  - It uses skill files with platform accessibility reference tables, so the agent picks documented APIs instead of guessing.
  - Its outputs are spec pages in Figma (anatomy, API, screen-reader behavior, motion) plus a JSON contract.
  - Visual intent stays in Figma, and the text contract is derived from it. Drift detection is on Uber's roadmap.
  - I couldn't verify uSpec's license, or that the `redongreen/uSpec` repo is officially Uber's.
- **Other approaches:**
  - W3C DTCG tokens hit their first stable version in October 2025. They are machine-checkable but cover only atomic values.
  - Storybook MCP exposes component manifests and a test-run tool.
  - Spec Kit is text-first with no visual model, and OpenSpec's main criticism is drift.

R1's lessons for Wisp:

1. Add a separate lightweight design-intent artifact in the DESIGN.md style (tokens plus prose plus Do/Don't), and keep `spec@1` for falsifiable behavior.
2. Let spec criteria reference tokens and visual references (a Figma node, a Storybook story, a screenshot) as evidence.
3. Offer an exploratory tier with no gate, promoted to a spec once stable.
4. Verify deterministically where possible.
5. Extend `scribe:spec-drift` to cover intent files.

## What the industry is doing

| Approach | What it is | Rigidity | Visual intent lives in |
|---|---|---|---|

| **Claude Design, Stitch, v0, Magic Patterns** | Generate variants, steer by comments and direct manipulation, and ingest your design system. | Very low | The rendered canvas |
| **Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenSpec** | Text-first spec, plan and tasks pipelines. | High | Nowhere. They have no visual model. |

## Patterns that recur

1. **Intent and behavior are kept separate.** DESIGN.md, uSpec and Storybook keep visual intent in tokens, prose or a design source. Behavioral contracts are a different artifact. Wisp's `spec@1` mixes the two and can only express the second.
2. **Render, then compare, is the standard verification loop.** Anthropic's own best-practices doc says to give the agent a way to verify its work, with a screenshot compared to the design for UI. Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools and Storybook's test tool all feed that loop. Your own sessions converged on it by hand. No Wisp plugin does it.
3. **Exploration is lightweight everywhere.** Even Anthropic's doc says to skip planning when the diff fits in one sentence, and that exploratory tasks may skip it. Practitioners say a vibe prototype is "your PRD, not your first product version."
4. **Specs hurt on taste-driven, moving UI.** Fowler's SDD review found Kiro turning a small bug into 4 stories and 16 criteria, and drift is a recurring complaint. OpenSpec answers with per-change deltas. This matches the churn on your SPEC-005 to 012.
5. **Two verification warnings.**
   - Visual regression tools show "unchanged," not "correct." The first agent render needs approval before it becomes a baseline (the agent's inference).
   - A clean axe run covers only about 57% of accessibility issues by volume, per Deque.
6. **Nobody has a real decision log.** Claude Design has no version history, and Figma Make users are asking for branching. This is a gap you could fill. Your "did you lose that decision" frustration is the industry-wide gap.
7. **Copy truth is unchecked everywhere.** AI UIs routinely contain invented stats and fake testimonials. Good checklists quote evidence and a location per finding, which is the check your case-study audit did by hand.

## What it means for Wisp

The proposals below mostly mirror the ones I made earlier from your sessions, and now they have outside precedent.

1. **A sketch mode with option files.**
   - Options are durable files with stable IDs and a status (open, parked, chosen, rejected) plus a one-line reason. That doubles as the decision log.
   - Render an option × brand × theme matrix from tokens, default to about 3 options, and keep them visibly low-fidelity.
   - Allow TBDs and use no gates.
2. **A design-intent artifact.** Use a DESIGN.md-style file (tokens plus prose plus Do/Don't) that is consumed and linted, not gated. Adopting the Google format outright would give you a lint CLI and Tailwind and DTCG export for free, but it is alpha.
3. **A promote path from sketch to spec.**
   - Derive the spec from the chosen prototype, and keep the prototype or its screenshots as the visual oracle.
   - Criteria would reference tokens and approved renders, not adjectives.
   - Use change-delta specs to limit churn, as OpenSpec does.
4. **A render-evidence artifact required by the implementation gate for UI work.**
   - Screenshots per viewport, theme and state, plus axe and Lighthouse output and console errors.
   - An unrendered UI would be reported as a coverage gap, never a pass.
   - This needs a browser capability kind added to recon, and could be built on Playwright or Chrome DevTools MCP.
5. **Optional design sources behind a capability-detected adapter.** Figma is one kind among screenshot, HTML, description and none. Many of your sessions were code-first, so Figma can't be a hard dependency. The agent also suggests token-use and component-reuse checks as a Code Connect equivalent for repos without Figma.
6. **Cheap deterministic checks.**
   - Token lint plus computed-style checks for hardcoded values.
   - Contrast and 44px target-size probes.
   - A copy-provenance diff of rendered text against source copy.
   - State that automated accessibility coverage is partial.
7. **Orchestration fixes.**
   - Plans should declare file ownership, with one writer for shared tokens, and cap parallel agents at about 3–5.
   - A post-merge render check would catch "intent conflicts" that merge cleanly.
   - Enforce the 3-retry gate cap.
   - Extend `scribe:spec-drift` to cover intent files.

## Gaps in the research

- No primary sources on Shopify, Airbnb, Vercel or Atlassian agentic front-end workflows. The hits were irrelevant.
- I couldn't verify uSpec's license or that its repo is officially Uber's, or DESIGN.md's per-agent integration docs.
- The Claude Design handoff bundle contents rest on one third-party blog.
- Prototype-to-spec has only blog-level support.
- Tempo, Relume and Uizard came back thin.

The detailed notes with URLs are in `/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/2d213021/tmp/` as `R1-design-md-uspec.md`, `R2-figma.md`, `R3-ai-design-tools.md` and `R4-verification-hardening.md`. They are deleted with the job unless I copy them somewhere durable.

## Suggested next step

Draft a design proposal for the smallest useful slice: a sketch skill with option files and a decision log, plus a promote path into muse, using a DESIGN.md-compatible intent file. Browser evidence for the implementation gate would be a separate follow-up. Do you want that, or would you rather start with the browser-evidence slice? I'd start with the sketch slice, since that is where your sessions lost the most time.

# uSpec Workflow Summary

## Core Process
uSpec follows a three-stage pipeline: **Extract** → **Compile** → **Render**. The system captures Figma components via plugin, generates canonical documentation, then optionally annotates designs.

## Commands & Skills
The primary command is `create-component-md`, which produces both JSON contract and Markdown guide. Additional `create-*` skills render specific sections (Anatomy, API, Properties, Color, Structure, Screen Reader, Motion) as Figma annotation frames. Motion is the exception—it reads from After Effects exports instead of the standard pipeline.

## Component.MD Contract
The system generates two complementary artifacts: a schema-valid JSON contract plus concise Markdown covering "API, structure, color, and screen-reader behavior." This dual format enables both machine validation and human-readable documentation in a single workflow.

## Accuracy Control
Deterministic extraction precedes generation. The uSpec Extract plugin captures "deterministic evidence" from components, which `create-component-md` then interprets and validates. This two-step approach aims to "save thousands of tokens per run and capture more component detail than live extraction."

## Supported Platforms
The system works with **Cursor**, **Claude Code**, and **Codex** agents, integrated via Figma MCP and a public plugin.

## Key Limitation
The workflow depends on extracting components once; `create-*` skills read generated Markdown rather than re-querying Figma, reducing redundant processing but requiring accurate initial capture.

content.text:
uSpec's main lesson for us is to extract facts from the real artifact instead of asking the model to write them. The model then does only the judgment that extraction can't. I checked Uber's blog post and the uSpec docs for this. Both are LLM-summarized fetches, so the quotes are accurate but I haven't read the pages in full.

## What uSpec is

- **The problem it solves.** Uber's design system spans 7 stacks (UIKit, SwiftUI, Android XML and Compose, React, Go, server-driven UI). It needed "hundreds of spec pages that all need to stay accurate." Specs that fall behind mean "engineering builds from assumptions."
- **Input.** A Figma component, plus optional human context about "states, variants, or platform-specific behavior that the agent can't infer."
- **Pipeline.** The docs describe it as Extract, Compile, then Render.
  1. A Figma plugin extracts "deterministic evidence" once.
  2. A `create-component-md` skill turns that into a schema-valid JSON contract plus a short Markdown guide.
  3. Optional `create-*` skills (anatomy, API, color, structure, screen reader, motion) render sections back into Figma as annotation frames.
- **Result.** A three-platform screen-reader spec "generates in under 2 minutes," and a whole system that took months can be done "in days."

## What we can learn

1. **Split extraction from judgment.**
   - Extracted programmatically: token names, variant values, component structure, layer hierarchy and variable modes.
   - Left to the LLM: accessibility semantics, token mapping across states, spec organization and platform behavior.
   - Our `muse:drafter` writes everything from a prose brief, so it can invent numbers. This is the cause of the stale 252px, 1180px and 224×42 values in your specs.
   - A "ground truth first" step would read the real tokens and the existing prototype or built components, and the drafter would then only add semantics.
2. **Constrain the model with reference tables, not instructions.**
   - uSpec's skills load platform accessibility references (VoiceOver modifiers, TalkBack semantics, ARIA roles) before analysis. "The agent doesn't guess at property names — it selects from documented APIs."
   - Muse has no such tables. It asks for "role, name, focus order" as free text. This is cheap to copy: an ARIA pattern reference (APG patterns, per-component keyboard maps) loaded before drafting.
3. **Extract once, then compile from the artifact.**
   - The `create-*` skills read the generated Markdown rather than re-querying Figma. That saves tokens and gives every downstream step the same facts.
   - We'd get the same effect from a single extraction artifact (tokens, states, measured geometry) that spec, plan and verification all read. That would avoid the contradictions the gate spent 51 calls chasing across SPEC-005 to 012.
4. **A dual-format contract.** Component.MD pairs a machine-validatable JSON contract with a human-readable guide. Our `spec@1` is JSON only. You couldn't judge it without pictures, so a rendered human view of each spec would help.
5. **Visual intent stays in the visual source.** Uber never tries to put appearance into the text contract. The text is derived from the design, and the design remains the source of truth. For us, the visual source is the prototype or approved screenshots, which fits the sketch-then-promote idea.
6. **Human-in-the-loop is minimal and targeted.** Uber asks only for what can't be inferred, then shows the result rendered in context for review. Our gate loops had the reverse shape: lots of automated back-and-forth, with a human who couldn't see the thing.
7. **Drift is the stated next step.** Uber lists drift detection and code-to-spec on the roadmap, so a team with a well-resourced design system hasn't solved it either. Our `scribe:spec-drift` already exists, so extending it to compare extracted facts with the spec is realistic.

## Where uSpec doesn't help us

- **It assumes a Figma-first workflow with a structured design system.** Uber's own caveats are that it needs well-structured Figma files and accurate tokens. Your sessions were code-first, so the extraction source would have to be built components, token files and rendered pages. The principle transfers. The tool doesn't.
- **It documents existing components.** It doesn't help with ideation or exploration, which is your main pain.
- **I could not verify its license** or that the GitHub repo (`redongreen/uSpec`) is officially Uber's. Check before depending on it.

## How I'd apply it

- **Ground truth step for muse.** Add a recon step that extracts token values, component props and measured geometry from the repo, a running page or a prototype into one facts file. The drafter cites it instead of inventing numbers.
- **ARIA and keyboard reference tables** that muse loads before drafting, like uSpec's accessibility references.
- **A human-readable rendering of each spec**, ideally with the prototype beside it, so approval isn't a wall of text.

The first item is the biggest. It addresses the stale-number problem directly and is useful whether or not we ever build sketch mode. Want me to fold it into the sketch-mode design proposal?

It catalogs ~165 "coercion techniques": prohibitions, tool-gating, validation loops, and exemplar (Incorrect/Correct) pairs.
  - Headline claim, from a search snippet and not verified by me: almost none of the surveyed systems ship llms.txt, Code Connect, or agent instruction files. Some "llms.txt" URLs return 404s or HTML shells.
  - shadcn/ui is the exception. It ships a bundled MCP (`npx shadcn@latest mcp`), an Agent Skill with hard "Critical Rules", a curated llms.txt (https://ui.shadcn.com/llms.txt), a CLI with `info --json` and `add --dry-run`, and an eval suite that regression-tests the skill's rules. The system page is at https://state-of-ai-in-design-systems.netlify.app/systems/shadcn-ui.
  - I did not check Radix, Material, Chakra, Ant, Mantine, Base UI, Spectrum or Primer individually. I rely on Kaelig's survey for them.
  
  **Anti-slop skills (primary repos).**
  - Hallmark (https://github.com/Nutlope/hallmark) picks a macrostructure and a theme, runs 57 slop-test gates, then a pre-emit self-critique. It has four verbs: build, audit, redesign, study. It documents no screenshot step.
  - avoid-ai-design (https://github.com/funboy322/avoid-ai-design) is the closest to a pipeline gate. It has a zero-dependency scanner (`detect.mjs`) with 67 deterministic patterns, P0/P1/P2 severity, and JSON output with exit codes for CI. It also names "second-order slop": cream plus terracotta, monochrome with one accent, and numbered 01/02/03 features. It writes a DESIGN.md to stop drift across pages.
  - taste-skill (https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill) has nine skills and three dials: DESIGN_VARIANCE, MOTION_INTENSITY, VISUAL_DENSITY. It also has a redesign-audit and a pre-flight check. Its star count is 46k in one source and 98k in another, so treat it as unverified.
  - Anthropic's frontend-design skill is the baseline. Before writing CSS it asks four questions (purpose, tone, constraints, differentiation) and commits to one bold aesthetic direction.
  - Practitioner skills: Emil Kowalski (motion), Jakub Krehel (typography and layout), indexed at https://craftwork.design/skills. That index is secondary.
  
  **How slop is controlled (consistent across sources).**
  - Ban lists for fonts, gradients and glassmorphism.
  - A named aesthetic direction picked before any code, plus explicit "rejection clauses" in the intent file.
  - Deterministic linters, which are better than prompt-only rules.
  - Self-critique gates before output.
  - Adpharm (https://www.theadpharm.com/insights/claude-design-without-the-ai-slop-look, secondary) recommends mixing two named aesthetic families and a nine-section DESIGN.md that includes rejection clauses.
  
  **Design-intent files.** DESIGN.md is the de facto convention. Explainers say it came from Google Stitch, with YAML tokens plus a prose rationale:
  - https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/design-md-ai/
  - https://github.com/voltagent/awesome-design-md
  - https://dev.to/aws-builders/agentsmd-skillmd-designmd-how-ai-instructions-split-into-three-layers-d0g (argues for AGENTS, SKILL and DESIGN as three layers)
  
  I found no STYLE.md or brand.md convention.
  
  **Exploration-first.** The closest primary source is Matt Pocock's `prototype` skill (https://github.com/mattpocock/skills). It builds throwaway prototypes, either a single HTML file or several UI variations toggled from one route. It sits between grill-me (requirements Q&A) and TDD/PRD. This maps well to a lightweight exploration mode that sits outside the spec-to-gate pipeline, with hardening afterwards. Secondary essay: https://newsletter.thelongcommit.com/p/the-prototype-is-a-question-not-a. Parallel-variant posts that use git worktrees exist (e.g. https://developer.upsun.com/posts/ai/git-worktrees-for-parallel-ai-coding-agents), but they are generic and not design-specific.
  
  **Visual QA / critique agents.**
  - The best concrete example is the Design Reviewer agent in TechNickAI/ai-coding-config (https://github.com/TechNickAI/ai-coding-config/pull/4/files). It uses Playwright at 1440, 768 and 375 widths and checks hierarchy and WCAG AA contrast. Findings are tiered by severity and written in user-impact language with screenshots.
  - The "Eyes" and "Visual Review" skills (https://mcpmarket.com/tools/skills/visual-feedback-loop-eyes, https://mcpmarket.com/tools/skills/visual-review-ui-inspection) are marketplace listings. Their quality is unverified.
  
  **Thin or unverified.**
  - I found no verified write-up of an explicit "explore without specs, then backfill specs and tests" design lifecycle.
  - I found no verified option-board technique from a named design-engineer practitioner.
  - Nothing turned up on STYLE.md or brand.md, or on Rauno Freiberg.
  - Conference talks, newsletters and Config content are largely uncovered. Most of what I found is aggregator-grade (marketplaces, listicles) rather than first-hand practitioner posts.
  
  **Patterns to borrow.**
  1. A prototype mode with a throwaway marker and an explicit promote step.
  2. A DESIGN.md with rejection clauses and tokens.
  3. A deterministic slop linter as a cheap gate, run before any LLM critique.
  4. A Playwright multi-viewport critic that reports severity-tiered findings.
  5. Skill-rule evals, as shadcn does.

| Company | What's public | Source quality |
|---|---|---|
| **Vercel** | An in-repo product-design skill with mode routing, plus a `design.md` brand file | First-party blog posts (Jun and Aug 2026) |

| **Microsoft Fluent** | A `/visual-test` skill that drives Storybook plus Playwright screenshots | Repo content, via the survey |

| **IBM Carbon** | Remote MCP, and a skill with a hard "never write Carbon code from memory" rule | First-party docs |
| **Spotify Encore** | A test framework scoring AI output against real components | Second-hand talk writeup only |

| **Airbnb, Netflix** | Nothing relevant | None. Netflix has only job postings. |

I found nothing public for Intuit or Duolingo. Pinterest's MCP post doesn't cover its design system. Linear, Stripe and Notion have only third-party DESIGN.md extractions.

## Findings most relevant to us

1. **Vercel's mode routing is the closest model to your exploration-versus-hardening need.**
   - Their product-design skill picks a mode first: *shape* (compare alternatives, no edits), *implement*, *review* (no edits unless asked), *copy*, or *harden* (keep direction, fix states and accessibility).
   - Exploration modes are read-only, and hardening is a separate mode with its own rules.
   - The skill's contract says never claim visual verification from code alone, and findings are graded P0 to P3.
   - Rule candidates stay pending until a human accepts them, and they never promote a single screenshot or comment into a rule.
2. **Atlassian's evidence argues against one big DESIGN.md.**
   - On the same login-screen task, a monolithic DESIGN.md used about 7.2M tokens against 3.75M for their MCP.
   - It also lost information when compressed and led agents to recreate components instead of importing them.
   - They recommend DESIGN.md only for art direction, quick prototyping and customer theming.
   - This refines my earlier suggestion. The design-intent file is still right for exploration and brand direction. Component facts should come from a lookup (a CLI or MCP) or from extraction, not from a big file.
   - Their CLI matched their MCP on speed and tokens, so a CLI-style lookup works anywhere there's a shell.
3. **Lint is the preferred gate.**
   - Salesforce requires its linter to pass before a skill emits code.
   - Primer makes `lint_css` a required final step.
   - Spectrum ships a deterministic, severity-weighted audit rubric.
   - Vercel pairs deterministic linters with evals that use hidden expected edits on unseen interfaces.
   - This matches R4's finding that our gates check spec consistency and never render or lint anything.
4. **"Never write from memory" is a hard rule.** Carbon, SLDS and Spectrum all say it. The reference material is the truth, not the model. This is the same lesson as uSpec's reference tables.
5. **Generated, routed, short context.**
   - Spectrum generates its skills and MCP content from the docs source on every deploy, so agent context can't drift from human docs.
   - Carbon's root AGENTS.md is 69 lines and acts as a router.
   - Vercel keeps a `coverage-gaps.md` listing where no standard exists, which is an honest record of what the agent shouldn't guess.
6. **Visual verification is per-component.** Fluent boots Storybook per component and drives Playwright screenshots. Spotify scores against real components. Nobody relies on a spec for visual correctness.
7. **Design tools keep a human approval step.** v0 requires you to approve the preview before it saves an ingested design system.
8. **Anti-"slop" controls.** From the earlier sweep: ban lists, a named aesthetic direction picked before any code, rejection clauses in the intent file, and deterministic scanners. The `avoid-ai-design` scanner has 67 patterns and CI exit codes.

## Caveats
- **Weak evidence.** The numbers are self-reported and the companies themselves caveat them: Atlassian's "34% faster," Vercel's "57% fewer failures" (their sample is far too small to conclude anything), and Atlassian's "20 minutes instead of 4–5 days."
- **Unreliable Airbnb material.** The only Airbnb AI material is through third-party summaries, and one talk is dated "November 2026," after today's date. I'd ignore it.
- **Claims S1 couldn't confirm.** The Shopify dev MCP "validating generated code" claim, because the fetched page didn't name specific tools. Also Tobi's April 2025 memo, seen only through press coverage.
- **Conflicting v0 dates.** Third-party launch dates for v0 Design Systems 2.0 conflict (Feb vs June 2026), and I found no Vercel blog post for it.
- **Unread pages.** The Medium and "Carbon for AI" pages returned 403, so those weren't read.
- **Coverage.** I found no first-party material on conference talks, Netflix engineering, Intuit or Duolingo.

## Changes to my recommendations

- **Add mode routing to the sketch design.** A Vercel-style entry point that picks *shape / implement / review / harden* first. Exploration modes would be read-only or sketch-only, and hardening would be separate. This gives us the "lightweight" and "rigid" modes you want without removing the pipeline.
- **Replace "one big intent file" with a small routed one.** Keep it for art direction and brand, with rejection clauses. Component facts come from extraction or a CLI lookup.
- **Prefer lint over gate prose.** For tokens, copy and slop patterns, a deterministic scanner is cheaper and more trustworthy than another LLM gate round.
- **Add a coverage-gaps file** (Vercel's idea) so the agent knows where no standard exists and asks instead of guessing.
- **Rule promotion needs human acceptance**, so a one-off preference in a session doesn't become a permanent rule.

The notes with URLs are in `/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/2d213021/tmp/` as `S1-shopify-airbnb-vercel-atlassian.md`, `S2-netflix-ibm-others.md` and `S3-community-practitioners.md`. They go away with the job unless I copy them somewhere durable.

## Suggested next step

I think we have enough evidence to stop researching and draft the design proposal. It would cover:

- A mode-routed `sketch` skill with option files, a decision log and a promote path into muse.
- A routed design-intent file.
- A ground-truth extraction step for specs.
- A render-evidence requirement plus lint-style checks for implementation gates.

Do you want that drafted as a document (and where it should live), or would you rather discuss the shape first?

result.output:
# TanStack Intent 0.5: Agent Skills Management

## What is TanStack Intent?

Intent is a CLI tool enabling library maintainers to package and ship "skills"—AI agent instructions—directly within npm packages. These skills travel with library versions, ensuring agents receive up-to-date guidance aligned with the code they're using. As the article states: "library maintainers can ship agent skills inside their npm packages. When the package is installed, the skills come along with it."

## Version 0.5 Changes

The 0.5 release shifts focus from initial skill authoring to ongoing maintenance. Key additions include:

- **Example validation** using TypeScript compiler
- **Source review workflow** tracking which library changes require skill updates
- **CI integration** with reusable GitHub checks
- **Repair command** for routine fixes

The philosophy: "It helps to solve the delivery problem. It doesn't, by itself, solve the maintenance problem."

## Skill Authoring & Packaging

Skills are authored in `SKILL.md` files within library repositories. They contain guidance, patterns, anti-patterns, and code examples. The setup command registers skills and prepares the repository:

```
npx @tanstack/intent@0.5.0 maintainer setup
```

Skills are versioned with their npm package, ensuring a 1:1 correspondence between package version and skill guidance—eliminating staleness from external documentation sources.

## Keeping Skills Synchronized with Code

Intent addresses staleness detection through multiple mechanisms:

**Example Validation:**
```
npx @tanstack/intent@0.5.0 validate
```

This command "checks fenced JavaScript and TypeScript examples in SKILL.md" using the TypeScript compiler, catching "missing exports, invalid options, type mismatches, and syntax errors."

**Source Review Workflow:**
The `maintainer review` command identifies guidance affected by source changes. Rather than asking "is this file old?" it poses the more practical question: "has someone checked this guidance against what changed?" Reviews are tied to specific source and skill versions, preventing repeated approvals of unchanged decisions.

**Repair Command:**
```
npx @tanstack/intent@0.5.0 repair --write
```

This applies mechanical fixes to frontmatter; suggested code changes require explicit review.

## CI & Maintenance Infrastructure

Intent includes "reusable GitHub checks for validation, generated-file drift, and pending source reviews." Problems surface in Actions summaries without automatically applying fixes—"the aim is to spend less time on mechanical corrections without hiding the decisions that still need a maintainer."

## Skill Discovery by Agents

The article doesn't detail agent discovery mechanisms explicitly, but implies skills are bundled and discovered locally. A notable performance improvement: "Agent hooks use the locally installed CLI when one is available instead of resolving a package through the registry at every session start."

## Skill Structure

While the article references `SKILL.md` as the storage format, it doesn't provide detailed structural specification. Skills contain examples, explanations, patterns, and anti-patterns—all tied to library features via fenced code blocks (JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, TSX).

## Philosophy & Lessons

The core lesson: "Maintainers already hold a lot of knowledge about how their libraries should be used. Skills give that knowledge a way to reach coding agents." The framework emphasizes that "skills belong in the development process" rather than existing separately, ensuring guidance stays current through regular maintenance cycles integrated into existing workflows.

content.text:
Yes. The article's main point is that delivering agent guidance is the easy part and keeping it current is the hard part. That is the same drift problem we keep hitting. This comes from one LLM-summarized fetch, so the quotes are accurate, but the article gives no detail on how agents discover skills or on a skill's structure.

## What Intent does

TanStack Intent is a CLI that lets library maintainers ship `SKILL.md` files inside their npm packages. The skills travel with the package version, so an agent gets guidance that matches the code it installed. The article says: "It helps to solve the delivery problem. It doesn't, by itself, solve the maintenance problem." Version 0.5 is about maintenance:

- **`validate`** compiles the fenced JS and TS examples in a skill with the TypeScript compiler. It catches missing exports, invalid options, type mismatches and syntax errors.
- **`maintainer review`** finds guidance affected by source changes. It asks "has someone checked this guidance against what changed?" instead of "is this file old?" Reviews are tied to specific source and skill versions, so an unchanged decision isn't re-approved.
- **`repair --write`** applies mechanical fixes to frontmatter only. Suggested code changes still need explicit review.
- **CI checks** cover validation, generated-file drift and pending source reviews. They surface problems in the Actions summary without auto-applying fixes. The aim is "to spend less time on mechanical corrections without hiding the decisions that still need a maintainer."

## What we can learn

1. **Version guidance with the thing it describes.** A skill that ships in the package matches the installed code, so it can't go stale from an external source. For us, design intent and component facts should live in the repo and move with the components, not in a spec that drifts separately. This supports the earlier finding that specs lagged prototypes by a day.
2. **Compile the examples.** Intent type-checks every code example in a skill. We could do the same for muse specs and any design-intent file. Token references, component names and prop names would be checked against the real tokens and exports, which would have caught the stale 252px, 1180px and renamed props before a human did.
3. **Staleness means "unreviewed since the source changed," not "old."**
   - Tie each review to the source version it covered. When a token file or component changes, flag only the guidance that touches it.
   - This is a better model for `scribe:spec-drift` than re-checking everything. It would also be cheaper than the repeated 51-call gate rounds.
4. **Split mechanical fixes from judgment.** `repair` fixes frontmatter automatically and leaves code changes for review. Our gate loops spent many rounds on wording and citation fixes, which a mechanical pass could have made, leaving the gate for real contradictions. This gives a concrete rule for the convergence control we lacked.
5. **CI surfaces, it doesn't auto-fix.** Problems go in a summary for a human decision, which is the pattern we want for render checks and copy checks.
6. **Tie the process to where the work happens.** The article says skills "belong in the development process." Maintenance is part of the normal change flow, not a separate chore.

## Where it applies to Wisp itself

This applies to Wisp's own plugins as well as to the sites. The `shared/references/` files and the muse docs we found already have a drift defect: three places point to a ranger accessibility taxonomy that doesn't exist. A Wisp equivalent of `validate` could check that every cross-reference in plugin docs resolves. `just check` already validates manifests and versions, so this would be a small extension.

## Limits

- Intent targets library maintainers shipping guidance to consumers. It doesn't address exploration, visual verification or design intent.
- The article doesn't explain how agents discover skills. It only says hooks use a locally installed CLI when one is available.
- It validates code examples with the TypeScript compiler, which doesn't cover visual correctness. It fits tokens and component APIs, not how a page looks.

## Where it fits in the proposal

It strengthens the maintenance side. I'd add it to the plan as: ground-truth extraction, version-tied reviews, compiled examples, and a mechanical-repair pass before any gate. That covers keeping things current after the sketch-to-spec path has produced them.

Want me to fold this into the design proposal along with the earlier findings?

Both model-guidance reports are in. Anthropic's guidance supports a lighter exploration mode and points to a few things in Wisp worth fixing first. OpenAI's guidance points the same way, but its evidence is thinner.

I haven't verified the guidance claims myself. M1 says it fetched the primary Anthropic pages, so those are stronger. M2's key OpenAI pages returned 403, so its OpenAI findings are weaker. I did verify the repo-side facts below.

## Anthropic (Claude 5 family)

Changes from the 4.x models:

- **Less scaffolding.**
  - The Fable 5 page says "Skills developed for prior models are often too prescriptive… and can degrade output quality." It says to steer with a brief instruction rather than enumerating behaviors.
  - Emphasis like "CRITICAL: You MUST" is overtriggered by newer models. It's rationed, not banned.
- **More literal instruction following.** Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 follow "only report high-severity issues" literally and report less. Anthropic's advice is to have scanners report everything with confidence and severity, then filter in a separate pass. That matches Wisp's scanner, adversary and gate split.
- **Effort controls beat prompt-level thinking instructions.**
  - Lowering effort "reduces thinking… more reliably than prompt instructions do," and "think carefully" lines should be deleted on Opus 5.5.
  - Haiku 5.5 now exists and is the first Haiku with effort levels, so Wisp's haiku recon tier should be re-checked.
- **Self-verification depends on the model.** Opus 5 verifies on its own, and explicit verify steps cause over-verification. Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 at low effort report "done" without a real check. Fresh-context verifier subagents beat self-critique.
- **Subagents.** Opus 5 and Fable delegate more readily, so Anthropic documents damping prompts and hard caps on spawn depth and concurrency.
- **Frontend.** Generic "avoid the AI look" instructions just swap one default for another. Anthropic says to name specific patterns to ban, or have the model "propose 4 distinct visual directions… ask the user to pick one."
- **Exploration is endorsed.** The docs say "Vague prompts can be useful when you're exploring" and that planning overhead can be skipped for small or exploratory work. For Sonnet 5.5: "When the user asks for ideas, options or a plan, give them that and stop."

## What it means for Wisp

**Still right:**
- The recall-then-filter split, with the gate in a fresh context.
- Schema-first JSON handoffs.
- Retry caps. Opus 5.5 guidance suggests capping automatic continuations at two or three, which matches our cap of 3.
- Lower effort for subagent roles.
- XML sections plus a short role line.
- Concrete, falsifiable gate criteria.

**Probably unnecessary** (inference, and it needs an ablation eval before I'd remove anything): the byte-identical constitution in every agent, long `<backstory>` prose, repeated MUST/ALWAYS, "double-check" text in Opus producers, and the full 5-part skeleton on tiny recon agents. Anthropic has no statement on EARS or rigid multi-part structures.

**Possibly harmful, in priority order:**
1. **The "reasoning" scratchpad fields.**
   - M1 says Fable, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 may decline prompts or tool descriptions that ask the model to write out its reasoning, and that server-side fallback does not retry them. The suggested fix is to rename the fields to `rationale`, `evidence` or `actions_taken`.
   - It's a big surface in this repo. 29 of 31 schemas have a `reasoning` field, all 44 agents mention reasoning or a scratchpad, and the constitution requires the field (`shared/constitution.md:242`). The muse drafter calls it a scratchpad that is "never forwarded downstream."
   - I haven't verified the refusal behavior itself. Before any rename, check the transcripts for refusals and test it on one agent.
2. **A default-fail gate paired with an adversary told to find problems.** Claude Code docs warn that "a reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound." That can push loops toward the retry cap, which matches the 51-call exit-gate churn. The fix is to require blockers to cite evidence and make "no findings" a valid pass.
3. **Qualitative filtering in producers** ("only real or confident issues") lowers recall.
4. **Agents spawning their own verifier subagents.** The orchestrator should own spawning.
5. **"Never X" rules with no stated reason.** Explained rules generalize better.

**Tiers:**
- Haiku 5.5 at low skips checks and stops early on long prompts, so keep recon prompts short and move to medium if recon misses files.
- Opus 5.5 at medium roughly matches Opus 5 at high, so start gates at medium and sweep upward.
- Fable 5.1 is worth trying on the hardest gates.

## OpenAI (GPT-6 and Codex)

The model details are mostly search summaries, so treat them as unconfirmed until checked in a browser.

- **Models.** The current family is GPT-6: Astra (Sep 3), Sol and Luna (Sep 22), and GPT-6.1 Sol (Sep 29, the Codex default). One fetched guide page confirms the model ids, that Astra and Sol don't support effort `none`, and that sampling parameters are removed.
- **Prompting.** Short outcome briefs with one or two hard rules, not step scripts. The model acts by default, so restraint has to be written as boundaries. Its testing guidance (skip tests for reversible, low-impact changes) fits your exploration instinct.
- **Codex features (fetched).** AGENTS.md is capped at 32 KiB combined. Subagents are TOML files with `developer_instructions`, and they inherit the parent's sandbox. Skills follow the open `SKILL.md` standard.
- **Implications for our Codex counterparts.**
  - Handoff schemas, gates and tiers carry over.
  - Codex wording should lead with outcome and boundaries.
  - Keep the constitution in AGENTS.md as a short pointer, because of the cap.
  - Never use effort `none`.
  - Enforce read-only through the sandbox, not the agent file.

## How this changes the plan

1. **Sketch mode now has direct support from both vendors.** One agent, no schema handoff, no gate, low or medium effort, output labelled non-binding. Add a stated assumptions list, a hard stop before implementation, a scratch-directory-only write guard, and a promotion path to weaver or scribe.
2. **Add a gate-hygiene pass.** Evidence-citing blockers, "no findings" as a valid pass, and mechanical fixes made outside the gate. This addresses the churn.
3. **Run a `mason:evaluate` ablation on the scratchpad rename and on constitution size**, before removing anything. That is the repo's own method for these decisions.
4. **Re-check the haiku tier** against Haiku 5.5.

## Remaining research gaps
- **Anthropic.** Not fetched: the multi-agent research, context-engineering and long-running-harness posts, the Claude Code skills, plugins and hooks pages, the model cards, the Claude Design article and the frontend-design SKILL.md.
- **OpenAI.** The launch pages and system cards need a browser. There's no frontend or vision guidance, and the Codex plugin manifest, hooks, worktrees and cloud-task docs weren't read. Check `dist/codex` against the current spec before acting.
- **Internal cost data.** Gate cost in tokens and time from the transcripts, to size the case for a lighter mode.

This works as an analogy, and it fits our problems well. Aviation phraseology is a mature design for unambiguous handoffs between parties who can't see each other's state. The caveat is that I'm answering from my own knowledge of ICAO practice (Annex 10 and 11, Doc 4444, Doc 9432) and haven't fetched or verified anything for this. If we use any of it in the constitution, I'd check the specifics against the documents first.

## The strongest mapping: IFR vs VFR

- **IFR** is controlled flight. You file a plan, get a clearance, and fly the procedure. Deviation needs approval, and the controller is responsible for separation.
- **VFR with a flight information service (FIS/AFIS)** is advisory. The service gives information (traffic, runway in use, weather) but issues no clearances and exercises no control. The pilot stays responsible for deciding and for separation.

Today the Wisp pipeline is IFR for everything. The sketch mode you want is VFR with a flight information service, where the agent offers information, options and warnings and you make the decisions. The useful part is how aviation handles the boundary:

- You can request an IFR clearance in the air, which is the promote path from sketch to spec.
- You can cancel IFR when conditions allow, which is a valid way to drop back to exploration.
- Which mode you're in is always stated explicitly. Nobody is ever unsure whether they hold a clearance. Our orchestrator once carried on past an "escalate" verdict with an "owner-directed gate pass," which is the kind of ambiguity aviation designs out.

## What to borrow

1. **A closed vocabulary with fixed meanings.**
   - The standard words are "affirm," "negative," "roger" (received, not "yes"), "wilco," "unable," "standby," "say again," "verify," "correction" and "disregard." "OK" is avoided because it's ambiguous.
   - Our gate churn was often wording residue, such as "AC-047's Active clause still reads 'transparent'" and wrong AC citations. A small fixed set of verdict and handoff words would cut that.
   - "Unable" is the key one. It is a respectful, final "I can't do that" with no failure attached, and our agents have no equivalent that doesn't read as a gate failure.
2. **Readback and hearback.**
   - The pilot reads back safety-critical items (clearances, runways, altimeter settings, headings). The controller must listen and correct any error. Both halves matter, because a readback nobody checks is theater.
   - For us, a drafter would restate each blocker in its own words before changing the spec, and the gate would check the restatement. That catches misread blockers early, and it targets the SPEC-008 style loops where each round's prescribed fix caused the next blocker.
3. **Procedures as named, published routes (SID/STAR).**
   - A standard instrument departure or arrival is a pre-agreed route with a name. The clearance says "cleared via the [name] departure," not a paragraph of waypoints.
   - It reduces radio load, and everyone knows the details because they were fixed beforehand.
   - Our skills are already named procedures. What we lack is naming the common variants, such as "sketch," "harden," "review" and "promote." Vercel's mode routing, which the earlier research found, is the same idea.
4. **Pre-defined fallbacks for lost contact.**
   - Every IFR flight has lost-communications procedures, so nobody improvises when contact is lost.
   - For us, a stalled agent, a hanging 130 KB spec write, or a failed task has no defined behavior. The B report counted 17 failed agent tasks and 32 "stalled" mentions. Each agent would carry a stated "if no response in N, do X."
5. **The missed approach.**
   - At the decision altitude, if the criteria aren't met you go around. It's a procedure, and you do not push on and hope.
   - This maps directly to the 3-retry cap. The go-around is pre-briefed, objective and not shameful. Aviation treats it as the correct outcome of a stable system, which our orchestrator did not (it kept going past retry 4 and 7).
6. **Authority is explicit, and the pilot in command keeps final authority.**
   - In an emergency a pilot may deviate from a clearance, but must declare it and tell the controller afterwards.
   - We could allow an orchestrator override only when it states the override, why, and what it skipped, as a logged event and not a silent decision. This fixes the "owner-directed gate pass" problem.
7. **Urgency tiers with fixed meaning.** "Pan-pan" and "mayday" are two levels with defined handling. Our P0–P3 findings serve the same purpose, but they only work if the definitions are fixed and shared across every agent.
8. **Information is separate from instruction.** An information service never says "turn left." It says what it knows. The sketch mode would offer options and observations, never binding instructions, and it would label them that way.

## Where it doesn't transfer

- **Phraseology exists because voice is noisy, ambiguous and slow.** Pronunciation rules ("niner," "fife") and brevity limits don't apply to text and JSON. The transferable part is the closed vocabulary and the confirmation discipline.
- **Aviation is rigid because the cost of error is lives.** That is the opposite of your exploratory phase. The mapping gives rigidity where it's earned and VFR-style discretion where it isn't. It doesn't justify gating everything.
- **Phraseology only works with training and enforcement.** Pilots drill it. Our agents follow whatever the prompt says, so the vocabulary has to be short enough to hold in the prompt. Anthropic's guidance already warns against long prescriptive scaffolding.
- **I'm leaning on a metaphor.** It organizes the problems well, but each borrowed idea should be tested against the transcripts and not adopted because it sounds right.

## How I'd apply it

- Define 8–10 standard handoff words with fixed meanings (`affirm`, `negative`, `unable`, `standby`, `verify`, `correction`, `wilco`) in the constitution, used across all agents and checked by `mason:audit-plugin`.
- Add readback to the drafter-and-gate correction loop.
- Name the modes explicitly (sketch / harden / review / promote), with a stated "cleared by" for any gated step.
- Add lost-contact and go-around rules: per-agent timeouts, and a hard stop that goes to a human at the retry cap.
- Require overrides to be declared and logged.

The first and fourth items would have the largest effect on the gate churn and stalls we measured. Want me to dig into the actual ICAO documents to verify the details, or fold this into the proposal as a short section?

content.text:
Yes, it has been measured. The savings are real but much smaller than the headline, quality seems to hold, and a plain "be concise" gets most of it. The sources are the repo's own eval, an independent single-task test, JetBrains's 86-task benchmark (which I only saw through search summaries) and one academic paper.

## What "Caveman" is

It's a Claude Code skill that makes the model answer in terse fragments by dropping articles, filler, pleasantries and hedging. Technical content and code blocks stay intact. The repo went viral, reportedly passing 94k GitHub stars in under four months. ([Enterprise DNA](https://enterprisedna.co/resources/ai-pulse/ai-pulse-2026-07-28-a-claude-code-skill-called-caveman-respond-in-terse-fragment/))

## What has been measured

| Source | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **The repo's own evals** ([evals](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/tree/main/evals)) | Three arms: no prompt, "Answer concisely," and the skill. One call per prompt, on Opus 5.5. Output tokens counted with tiktoken. | Headline: ~65% output-token reduction (range 22–87%) over 10 prompts. The honest comparison is skill vs plain "concise." The repo admits the tokenizer is only an approximation, single runs lack statistical power, and the fidelity check only sees what its regexes test. |
| **Independent test** ([DEV Community](https://dev.to/nazecode/i-measured-the-viral-talk-like-a-caveman-token-saver-a-two-word-prompt-got-most-of-it-118a)) | One C# debugging task, 3 runs per variant, answers compiled and run. | "Be concise." −29%, caveman −43%, maximum compression −64%. All variants produced correct code. The author stresses it's one task. |
| **JetBrains** ([blog](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/07/speak-to-ai-agents-like-cavemen-tosave-tokens/)) | Paired A/B on SkillsBench with 86 real software-engineering tasks in Claude Code. | About 8.5% output-token savings, with the skill forced on. An early 10-task slice showed ~30%, and the figure fell as the sample grew. No detectable quality degradation: some tasks better, some worse, most tied. |
| **Other write-ups** ([BetterStack](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/caveman-llm/), [Mantel](https://mantelgroup.com.au/reducing-ai-token-consumption-caveman-method/), [InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4193775/talk-like-a-caveman-prompts-save-tokens-but-far-less-than-promised.html)) | Various. | Real coding tasks landed around 14–21%. Community reproductions are cited at 30–50% in normal use. |

JetBrains's page returned 403 when I fetched it, so its details come from search summaries and secondary coverage. I didn't read the other write-ups in full.

## What this tells us

- **The savings shrink as the work gets agentic.**
  - Chat answers are mostly prose, so terseness helps. In agent work, output is dominated by tool calls, code and diffs, which the style can't compress.
  - That is why ~65% became ~8.5%.
  - JetBrains's result is the most credible for our use case.
- **Plain "be concise" gets most of it.** Several independent testers found that, and the repo's own methodology concedes the point by using it as the baseline. A short instruction beats a long skill that costs input tokens every session. One test put the skill's break-even at about 10 answers.
- **Quality seems to hold, with thin evidence.**
  - JetBrains found no detectable degradation.
  - A separate paper, [Brevity Constraints Reverse Performance Hierarchies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00025), found that brevity constraints improved large-model accuracy by up to 26 points on some benchmarks. That is a different setup (benchmark questions, 31 models) and doesn't test caveman or agentic work. A related result I saw only in search summaries found a 27.7% math accuracy drop for GPT-3.5 under concise chain-of-thought. Brevity can help or hurt depending on the task.
- **None of it measures what matters most to us.** Output tokens were a minority of our gate cost. The 51 `muse:exit-gate` calls were expensive because of rounds and the specs read each time (input), not verbosity. And no study looked at terse style inside structured handoffs.

## What it means for Wisp

1. **Don't adopt caveman-speak for specs, plans or gate verdicts.**
   - The value of those artifacts is unambiguous wording. Dropping articles and connectives is the wrong trade there.
   - Muse's auditor already flags unnecessary prose as a defect. What we want is precision, which is why the aviation phraseology idea is the better version. That is a closed vocabulary, not a degraded register.
2. **Use plain brevity where it's harmless.** Candidates are the `reasoning` or `rationale` fields, status narration, and subagent reports to the orchestrator. The constitution already asks for proportionate scratchpads and no preambles (`shared/constitution.md:196`). A short "be concise" line may be enough, and it would cost nothing.
3. **If we want the savings, measure them in our own setting.** `mason:evaluate` is built for this. The sketch should have three arms, as the caveman eval does (baseline, plain concise, and the skill or style), run on a fixed task such as a muse draft-and-gate round. Count input and output tokens and check gate outcome, not output tokens alone.
4. **Watch the newer models.** Anthropic's guidance (from the earlier M1 report) says lowering effort and dropping prescriptive scaffolding does more than prompt tricks. A terseness instruction is an output-style knob and not a reasoning one, so don't expect it to fix gate cost.

## Caveats

- The headline numbers are self-published. JetBrains's 86-task figure is the only large independent one, and I could only see a summary.
- Savings depend on the model and task type, and most testing is on Claude Code with Sonnet or Opus.
- Nobody has measured terse style inside JSON handoffs or multi-agent loops.

I'd treat caveman as a minor optimization for narration and not a lever for the problems we found. The big levers remain gate churn, spec-versus-visual drift and the missing exploration mode. If you want it evaluated on our own agents, the three-arm eval is a cheap first use of `mason:evaluate`.

Sources:
- [Enterprise DNA](https://enterprisedna.co/resources/ai-pulse/ai-pulse-2026-07-28-a-claude-code-skill-called-caveman-respond-in-terse-fragment/)
- [caveman/evals](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/tree/main/evals)
- [DEV Community measurement](https://dev.to/nazecode/i-measured-the-viral-talk-like-a-caveman-token-saver-a-two-word-prompt-got-most-of-it-118a)
- [JetBrains](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/07/speak-to-ai-agents-like-cavemen-tosave-tokens/)
- [InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4193775/talk-like-a-caveman-prompts-save-tokens-but-far-less-than-promised.html)
- [BetterStack](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/caveman-llm/)
- [Mantel Group](https://mantelgroup.com.au/reducing-ai-token-consumption-caveman-method/)
- [Brevity Constraints (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00025)

Playwright got through the 403, and the full post confirms and sharpens what I reported from search summaries. I've corrected two details below.

## What JetBrains tested

- **Harness and agent:** Harbor 0.17, Docker-sandboxed trials, Claude Code 2.1.200 in headless mode.
- **Model:** `claude-sonnet-5` at low reasoning effort. I earlier assumed a bigger model, and that was wrong. Low effort matters here because the model already thinks little.
- **Benchmark:** SkillsBench, 86 of 87 tasks, each auto-graded 0–1 by its own tests with partial credit possible.
- **Arms:** stock Claude Code vs Caveman forced on every reply with an instruction line ("Use caveman mode…"). Same tasks, model, settings and budget per arm.
- **Volume:** 3 runs, about 240 billed trials, about $106.

## Results

1. **Saving is about 8.5%, not 65%.**
   - Output tokens fell from 592k to 542k over 82 clean pairs.
   - The 10-task smoke run showed −29.5%, which didn't replicate. The 10-task re-run with 3 runs each showed −6.7%.
   - Their explanation: agent output is mostly code, diffs, tool calls and exact error strings, which the skill correctly leaves verbatim. Only the narration between tool calls gets compressed, "and there is not much of it."
2. **No detectable quality difference.** Of the 82 pairs, 64 tied, 10 scored higher with the skill and 8 scored lower. Sign test p = 0.82. Average score was 0.326 for baseline vs 0.311 with the skill.
3. **Cost savings are fragile.**
   - Expected saving is about 10%, but the raw totals showed the skill arm 11.6% more expensive ($40.60 vs $36.39).
   - One dependency-audit task crossed the 200k long-context pricing tier in the skill arm and billed $8.29 vs $0.33, which accounts for the entire inversion. The same task produced a $3.25 outlier in the baseline arm on an earlier run.
4. **It's a ceiling.** The skill is user-activated, so JetBrains forced it on. Auto-triggered usage saves equal or less.

Their recommendation is "use it if you like it," but don't expect more than a high-single-digit percentage.

## Corrections to my earlier summary

- I described the benchmark as running on "Opus 5.5" in the repo's own eval and left JetBrains's model unstated. JetBrains used Sonnet 5 at low effort.
- The "86 tasks" figure is 82 paired tasks in the analysis, since four were excluded as unclean pairs.
- Everything else I reported matches the page.

## Lessons for our own evals

- **A small first run misleads.** The early −29.5% dissolved with scale, and a scary early quality gap shrank to noise. JetBrains's own advice is "Never trust a k=1 eval." Their headline run was still k=1 across 86 tasks, so the sign test and the larger sample carry the result, not repetition.
- **Pair the runs** on the same tasks and compare against a fair baseline.
- **Price outliers can flip a result,** so report cost with and without them.
- **Use task outcomes, not style, as the quality measure.**

Our `mason:evaluate` design should follow that shape: paired, multi-run, outcome-graded.

## Two other JetBrains posts worth reading

The page's sidebar links two posts relevant to us:
- **"Does 'rtk' skill really cut agent tokens by 60–90%? We tested it."** Your global CLAUDE.md uses RTK (Rust Token Killer) with that same 60–90% claim, so this test applies directly to your setup.
- **"How Netflix Made AI Coding Agents More Efficient with JetBrains IDE Intelligence"** (Oct 15, 2026). It claims 20–30% efficiency gains. It is also a rare Netflix data point, which we couldn't find earlier.

content.text:
I read both JetBrains posts in full through Playwright. The first one, on rtk, applies directly to your setup, since your global CLAUDE.md uses it. The Netflix post turned out to be about code intelligence, not design.

## rtk (Rust Token Killer)

JetBrains ran the same paired benchmark as for Caveman. The setup was Claude Code 2.1.201 with `claude-sonnet-5` at low and high effort, SkillsBench with 86 tasks, and rtk v0.43.0 installed exactly as `rtk init -g` ships it (binary, PreToolUse hook and RTK.md). That is the same install your CLAUDE.md describes. Total spend was about $320 over 425 billed trials.

| | Claimed | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Token cut | −60% to −90% | Fresh input tokens changed by +3.2% (low effort) and +4.3% (high effort), both within noise |
| Cost at low effort | Lower | **+7.6% more expensive** per task (80 tasks, p = 0.004), with 13.8% more turns and 14.3% more cache reads |
| Cost at high effort | Lower | No difference (+0.1%, p = 0.99) |
| Task quality | Unchanged | Unchanged: 5 better, 4 worse, 71 tied at low effort (p = 1.0) |

JetBrains's explanation:

- **A structural ceiling of about 3%.** Of 1,056 shell commands replayed from 83 baseline transcripts, only a third were something rtk can rewrite. Half were `python3`, project scripts or loops with no rule, and the rest use shell syntax rtk skips on purpose. Claude Code's built-in Read and Grep tools bypass the Bash hook entirely, and rtk's README admits this. So only about a fifth of tool output was compressible, and even squeezing all of it by 70% caps out near 3%.
- **The cost increase** appears to come from sessions running longer. More steps mean the model re-reads its history more times, and most of the bill is cached re-reads. Heavily rewritten task pairs cost about 24% more, versus 5% for pairs the hook barely touched. JetBrains found no single villain, just a few broken rewrites (compound `find` predicates), some compression-induced re-reads and ordinary variance.
- **`rtk gain` is not your bill.** Its own analytics reported 96.2 million tokens saved while the measured bill went up. It counts the full raw output as the counterfactual (one `cat` of a 1.2 MB file logged 320k "saved" tokens, though Claude Code would have truncated it anyway). It also estimates tokens as characters ÷ 4, while most input cost is cached re-reads billed at a tenth of the price.
- **One real compatibility failure.** The rtk binary refused to start in one task's image because it needs a newer glibc.

JetBrains's verdict: "Honest engineering, wrong counterfactual." The filters are real and the quality is fine. The advertised savings had nowhere to live in agentic coding. Their general lesson: "a tool's self-reported savings are a claim about its counterfactual, not about your bill."

**Limits of applying it to you:**
- The benchmark is SkillsBench tasks on Sonnet 5, not your Playwright-heavy front-end sessions. Browser output isn't touched by rtk either way.
- The full runs were k=1, and 80 tasks can only rule out large effects. JetBrains says catching a subtle few-point quality shift would need about 700 runs per side.
- Your own sessions might differ. I haven't touched your rtk config, and I wouldn't change it on this evidence alone. If you want to know, the clean test is to compare paired real tasks with the hook on and off, using actual billed cost and not `rtk gain`.

## Netflix + JetBrains code intelligence (Oct 15, 2026)

- **What it is.** Netflix's Application Development Platform, GenAI Platform and Agentic SDLC teams plugged JetBrains's headless code-intelligence engine into Claude Code and Codex. It targets Java and Kotlin navigation, especially across compiled JAR boundaries, where agents otherwise unzip, decompile and grep. Netflix built the daemon (to keep the index warm) and CLI (to make the language server callable by an agent) because JetBrains hadn't shipped them.
- **Results.** Typically 20–30% more efficient (average of token and time savings), up to about 65% in the best case, with correctness held or improved in every run. Gains were largest for the strongest model at high effort.
  - Tested on Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.
  - Two codebases: an internal Spring Boot service and Netflix's open-source DGS Framework.
  - Two task types: navigation questions and end-to-end tasks.
  - A crashed or thrashing task was excluded from both arms.
  - Correctness was judged against a reference change set (LLM-as-judge for end-to-end tasks, deterministic scoring for navigation).
- **Caveats.** It's a JetBrains-hosted case study, so treat it as vendor-curated. The 65% best case is navigation with the strongest model, and the end-to-end gains were roughly 21–30%. Netflix plans to repeat this for Python, TypeScript and JavaScript, and Go.

JetBrains's point that agents need answers in terms of symbols, diagnostics and test relations, not cursor positions, has a front-end equivalent. # Decision Records

Decide whether an architectural choice needs a durable record, and write the record so a later reader with no memory of the discussion does not silently reverse it. A record preserves the reason behind a decision, so nobody accepts it blindly or reverses it blindly.

## Write one only when both gates pass

- **Architectural:** the choice sets a boundary, a model, a direction, or a rule that several changes must respect.
- **Expensive to reverse or not obvious from the code:** a reader who sees only the code would plausibly undo it, or undoing it would be costly.

One decision per record. A choice that fails a gate belongs elsewhere.

| Fact | Home |
| :--- | :--- |
| Architecture, model, direction, decision, rejected alternative | Decision record in `docs/adr/` |
| Rule for every session: command, invariant, style, routing | `AGENTS.md` |
| Required behavior | Spec |
| How the system works today | Docs |
| Why one change was made | Commit message |
| Personal preference or correction for one repository | Agent memory, uncommitted |

Agent memory is unshared and goes stale, so a decision never lives only there.

## Form

Title, status, context, decision, options considered, consequences. Each rejected option carries its "because". Keep a record to one or two pages. Records written before this form may state the alternatives inside the context; leave them as written.

Add an `Enforced by` line only when a test, lint, type, or hook enforces the decision. A decision that a check can enforce should have the check; the record explains why it exists.

Add one line to the `docs/adr/README.md` index in the form `Do not <X> without a new ADR`, for a decision an agent could undo without noticing.

## Prose

Keep the causal "because" and the rejected alternative. Cut narration of the discussion, restated code, and hedging. Write one paragraph per line; do not hard-wrap.

## Status and change

Do not rewrite an accepted record's context, decision, or options; the reasoning at the time is what the record preserves. Update its status and links, and fix errors that do not change its meaning. To change a decision, write a new record that supersedes it and mark the old one superseded; the old record stays. Keep the active set small by writing records only for decisions that pass both gates.

## Refutation and disposition
